blog_personal_06_glm.text:
Co-parenting across time zones: managing school schedules from Berlin and Toronto

When Marcus took the teaching position at Humboldt University in September 2023, we knew our co-parenting arrangement was about to get complicated. He moved to Berlin, and I stayed in Toronto with our two kids, Elena (11) and Theo (8). Six hours of time difference doesn't sound like much until you're trying to coordinate a parent-teacher night.

After eighteen months of this, here is what we've figured out.

Everything goes into one shared Google Calendar: school events, swim practice at Wallace Emerson Community Centre, Theo's Wednesday speech therapy at 4 p.m. Toronto time. If it's not in the calendar, it doesn't exist. Marcus checks it with his morning coffee at 7 a.m. Berlin time, which is 1 a.m. for me, so he catches anything from my evening before I've woken up.

We split who attends what. Marcus can't sit in the gymnasium at Earl Grey Public School, but he joins parent-teacher interviews by video, usually at 8 or 9 p.m. his time. Elena's teachers have been generous about offering early slots. For things that need a body in the room, like the winter concert and March break pickup, he books flights. He's been back four times, staying in a rental near us on Dovercourt Road.

The kids have "Berlin dinner" every Tuesday and Friday. That's 2:30 p.m. for Marcus, so he eats lunch while they eat dinner and they talk about their week. Theo likes to show him LEGO builds over the camera. Elena mostly rolls her eyes but never misses a session. We don't schedule playdates over it.

The hard parts are real. When Theo had the flu last February and I was up all night, Marcus felt useless 6,600 kilometres away. He can still help, though. He handles the online tasks from abroad: ordering school supplies, booking Theo's therapy appointments, researching March break camps.

Time zone math has become the kids' odd skill. Theo can convert Toronto to Berlin in his head faster than I can. Europe switches to daylight saving two weeks before North America in spring, so for a fortnight the difference is five hours and everyone gets confused.

This isn't the arrangement we pictured when we separated in 2021. But Elena recently told her school counselor she has "a dad in two countries," and she said it like it was a superpower. I'll take that.

If you're doing something similar, use a shared calendar, protect your call times, and split the invisible labour by continent. It's not perfect, but it's ours.

blog_personal_04_luna.text:
On January 8, 2025, at age 51, I laced up my running shoes with one goal: to finish my first half marathon after a knee replacement.

A year earlier the idea would have sounded ridiculous. In March 2024, I had my right knee replaced after years of arthritis made stairs, long walks, and even getting out of the car miserable. Recovery was slow and humbling. My physical therapist, Elena Morales, started me with five-minute walks around my neighborhood in Sacramento, California. By June, I could walk two miles without stopping. By September, I was riding a stationary bike and doing strength exercises three times a week.

Running still felt off-limits until my friend Marcus mentioned the Davis Turkey Trot Half Marathon, scheduled for November 27, 2025. "You don't have to run every step," he said. "You just have to train consistently."

So I began with a walk-run plan: one minute of jogging followed by two minutes of walking, repeated for 20 minutes. My first workout covered just 1.4 miles, and my knee was swollen afterward. I iced it, called Elena, and learned that progress is not the same as pushing through pain.

Now I train four days a week. Tuesdays are easy walk-runs, Thursdays are strength sessions, Saturdays are longer, slower outings, and Sundays are for stretching and recovery. I increase my long distance by no more than half a mile each week. In February, I completed three miles. By April, I reached six. Last Saturday, I finished nine miles along the American River Parkway in two hours and eleven minutes.

I'm not chasing a personal record. I want to cross the finish line in Davis before the course closes, preferably smiling and still able to walk afterward. My pace will be slower than it was when I was 30, mostly because I never ran when I was 30. But every mile feels like proof that my body can still surprise me.

At 51, with a titanium knee and a very patient training plan, I'm learning how to start over.

blog_personal_02_sonnet.text:
The garage smells like PB Blaster now, permanently, I think. I picked up the bike on August 2nd from a guy in Hillsboro named Russ who'd had it sitting under a tarp since 2011: a 1978 Honda CB750K with 31,400 miles, matte with dust, $1,400 cash. The odometer cable was seized, the carbs were varnished solid, and a family of something had been living in the airbox. Classic first-owner-in-a-decade situation.

Week one was just degreasing. I went through four cans of Simple Green and an entire Saturday just getting eleven years of grime off the engine cases before I could even see what I was working with. Turns out the cases are in great shape: no cracks, no stripped threads, just cosmetic corrosion on the fin edges.

Week two I pulled the carb bank (four Keihin CV carburettors) and soaked them in a Berryman's dip for three days. Rebuilt them with a kit from CB750 Supply, $89 for all four sets of gaskets, O-rings, and float valves. That was the most satisfying afternoon of the whole project so far; watching float bowls that were crusted shut open up clean again.

Money so far, since I'm tracking it in a notebook on the workbench:
- Bike: $1,400
- Carb rebuild kit: $89
- Battery (YB9-B, since the old one was basically a brick): $34
- New fuel lines and inline filter: $22
- Degreaser, brushes, gloves, shop rags: about $60
- NGK spark plugs, set of four: $18

Total: $1,623 as of tonight, September 20th.

Compression tested at 145, 148, 142, and 140 psi across the four cylinders, which for a 48-year-old air-cooled engine felt like winning the lottery. I haven't tried to start it yet. That's the goal for next weekend, once I've got fresh gas in the tank and the points gapped to spec. My neighbor Dave, who's rebuilt two of these himself, keeps telling me not to rush the first kick. I'm rushing it anyway.

blog_personal_10_luna.text:
When we began homeschooling our son, Eli, in September 2022, he was eight years old and reading at roughly a first-grade level. Dyslexia made every worksheet feel like a test he had already failed. He could explain the water cycle with a detailed drawing, but reading a short paragraph about it left him exhausted and embarrassed.

We tried three popular language arts programs during that first year. One relied heavily on independent reading, and another moved through spelling lists too quickly. Neither lasted more than six weeks. The curriculum that finally worked for us was All About Reading Level 2, paired with All About Spelling. The lessons were short (about 20 minutes each) and completely explicit about phonograms, syllables, and blending. Eli used letter tiles, tapped out sounds on the table, and read decodable books instead of guessing from pictures. By February 2023, he was reading simple chapter books aloud without shutting down.

For writing, we used Institute for Excellence in Writing's Primary Arts of Language. I appreciated that it separated the physical act of writing from the work of generating ideas. At first, Eli dictated his answers to me while I typed them. Gradually, he copied one sentence, then two, and eventually wrote short paragraphs. His favorite assignment was retelling "The Three Little Pigs" from the wolf's point of view.

Math was less of a struggle, but word problems were difficult because reading interfered with showing what he knew. Math-U-See worked well because it was hands-on and predictable. We spent nearly two months on multiplication with colorful blocks before moving to written equations. I read every word problem aloud, and he was allowed to draw the problem or explain his reasoning verbally.

The biggest change was slowing down. We school for about three focused hours each morning, with movement breaks every 25 minutes. We also stopped comparing our progress with the local school calendar. In May 2024, Eli read an entire 120-page adventure book independently. It took him nearly three weeks, but he finished it and immediately asked for the sequel.

Dyslexia has not disappeared, and homeschooling has not become effortless. But the right curricula gave Eli tools instead of pressure, and they helped him see himself as capable.

# How I saved $4,200 on three weeks in Portugal without roughing it

When I booked my trip to Portugal this past January, the sticker price should have been around $6,800. I paid about $2,600 total.

### Flights: $1,850 saved

I had 68,000 Chase Sapphire Preferred points and a stash of United miles from work travel over the past two years. In mid-September, Chase offered 25% extra points on transfers to United, which gave me enough for a round-trip saver award from Newark to Lisbon. I paid $121 in taxes and fees for a ticket that was selling for $982 in February, my travel dates.

Timing helped. I flew out January 9th and returned January 30th. Post-holiday, mid-winter fares to Europe from the Northeast drop dramatically, and the same itinerary in June was pricing at over $1,400.

### Accommodation: $1,600 saved

I split my three weeks between Lisbon (8 nights), Porto (6 nights), and Lagos in the Algarve (7 nights). Instead of hotels, I booked apartments through Booking.com in January, peak off-season, when owners are hungry for any booking. My one-bedroom apartment in Lisbon's Alfama district was $54 a night. A comparable June rate was around $150.

In Lagos, I found a guesthouse with an ocean-view room for $47 a night, breakfast included. I booked it through the Chase travel portal with my Sapphire card, which earned another 5% back in points.

### Everything else: $750+ saved

- Museums: The Lisbon Card (€42 for 72 hours) covered the Jerónimos Monastery, Belém Tower, and public transit, about €60 in value.
- Off-season tours: A Douro Valley wine tour from Porto cost €55 instead of the €85 summer price, and there were only six of us instead of a full van.
- Food: In January I didn't need a reservation at Taberna da Rua das Flores in Lisbon. I walked in on a Tuesday and got the same dinner without the tourist markup.

### The trade-offs

It rained four days in Porto. Some beach restaurants in Lagos were closed, and the days were short, with sunset around 5:30pm. Still, Lisbon hit 60°F most afternoons, and I had Sintra's Pena Palace nearly to myself on a Wednesday morning. In summer there's a two-hour line.

### The math

Flights saved $1,850, lodging $1,600, and tours and attractions $750, for a total of $4,200. That's enough to fund my next trip, which I'm already plotting. Greece in November, anyone?

Dear Professor Martinez,

I have a question about how to interpret the Q3 regression results in my economics term paper, "Minimum-Wage Changes and Part-Time Employment in California, 2012-2023."

My model estimates that a 10% increase in the real minimum wage is associated with a 0.8% decline in part-time employment (coefficient = -0.080, p = 0.03). It controls for county fixed effects, year fixed effects, unemployment, and industry composition. I also cite Freakley (2021), which reports no statistically significant employment reduction after minimum-wage increases. The paper currently describes my result as "consistent with a modest negative employment effect," and I worry that this contradicts Freakley.

Should I present the difference as a contradiction, or attribute it to differences in data and methodology? Freakley uses national quarterly data from 1990 to 2018. I use annual county-level data for California from 2012 to 2023 and look only at part-time workers. My coefficient also becomes statistically insignificant when I exclude 2020 and 2021, which suggests that pandemic-related labor-market disruption may be driving the result.

Would you recommend revising the discussion to emphasize these limitations and avoid claiming a direct disagreement with Freakley?

Jordan Lee

essay_opinion_09_glm.text:
I've been going to the Met since I was nine years old, when my grandmother handed over a couple of dollars and we spent the whole afternoon in the Egyptian wing. A kid from Queens could stand in front of the Temple of Dendur and feel like the whole history of the world belonged to her too.

That feeling is getting harder to afford. In August 2022, the Met raised mandatory admission for out-of-state visitors from $25 to $30. In 2025 it went to $35, among the most expensive museum tickets in the country. New York residents can still pay what they wish, in theory, but the policy hides behind a wall of fine print. The kiosks now lead with the full price. You have to know the workaround exists, and you have to be willing to tell a staffer, out loud, that you'd like to pay a dollar. For a family of four from the Bronx, that is an audition, not a discount.

The Met's leadership defends the hikes with simple math: post-pandemic costs, insurance, climate control for two million objects. It's also true that the museum's endowment doesn't stretch as far as it once did. But look at who is being asked to close the gap. It isn't the trustees who mingle at gala dinners, or the tourists, for whom $35 is a rounding error on a $600 hotel night. It's the busload of teenagers from Newark, the nanny on her day off, and the art student who used to come sketch on Tuesdays.

A city can be judged by what its poorest residents can get into. Central Park is free. The Staten Island Ferry is free. The Met was supposed to be in that tradition: a public institution on public land, held under a lease with the city and partly supported by public money. A $35 gate says something different, that culture is a product and you are a customer.

The fix isn't complicated. London's British Museum and the Tate have kept admission free through economic cycles far worse than this one, because Britain decided access was non-negotiable. The Met could do the same, with real endowment campaigns and real city support, instead of quietly pricing out the people whose museum this is supposed to be.

If it doesn't, someday soon a nine-year-old from Queens will stand outside those steps on Fifth Avenue, and her grandmother will look at the ticket price and keep walking. The Met and the city will both be poorer for it.

essay_student_03_glm.text:
The Ford Model A, introduced in December 1927, helped speed the growth of American suburbs in the late 1920s and 1930s. Production of the aging Model T ended in May 1927, and Ford shut down its plants for six months to retool. The Model A debuted on December 2, 1927, and was faster, safer, and more comfortable than the car it replaced. Prices ran from about $385 for the Roadster to roughly $1,400 for the Town Car, so middle-class families could still afford it, and it was refined enough for longer daily drives. More than four million Model A's were sold by 1931. By 1930 the United States had over 23 million registered automobiles for a population of about 123 million.

Cars changed the geography of American cities. A worker who once had to live within walking distance of a factory or streetcar line could now commute ten or fifteen miles. The Model A's top speed of around 65 miles per hour, against the Model T's 40 to 45, made suburban commutes to cities like Detroit, Chicago, and Los Angeles practical for the first time. Developers responded. In Los Angeles, sprawling subdivisions expanded along new arterial roads. On Long Island and in Westchester County, New York, developers of the communities that preceded Levittown marketed homes to commuters who owned cars. Billboards of the era pitched houses "a twenty-minute drive from downtown."

Government policy pushed in the same direction. The Federal Aid Highway Act of 1921 had already created a system of paved primary roads, and local governments added paved suburban streets, often paid for with municipal bonds that assumed growth built around the automobile. Shopping changed too. Roadside businesses, diners, and early shopping centers like Kansas City's Country Club Plaza (opened 1923, expanded through the late 1920s) served customers who arrived by car instead of streetcar.

The Great Depression slowed construction after 1929, but suburbanization continued in the same direction. The Model A sat between the utilitarian Model T and the mass automobility of the postwar era. It made reliable, comfortable car ownership normal for millions of ordinary families, and for many of them the ideal home shifted from a row house near the trolley to a detached house on a suburban lot with a driveway out front.

essay_student_19_luna.text:
Kant argues that lying is always morally wrong because it treats other people as tools instead of as rational individuals who deserve the truth. In his famous example, a murderer asks whether an innocent person is hiding in your house. Kant still says you should not lie, because morality depends on universal rules and not on predicting consequences. A lie can also produce unexpected harm and weaken trust in everyone's promises.

A lifeguard's dilemma suggests that protecting someone may sometimes justify deception. Imagine that on July 14, 2026, at Santa Monica State Beach, lifeguard Elena Ramirez sees a panicked child named Marcus struggling in a strong rip current. Marcus's younger sister, Sofia, is on the shore and begins running into the water to save him. Elena knows Sofia cannot swim well. If Elena tells Sofia, "Marcus is safe; stay where you are," even though he is still in danger, she may be lying to prevent a second drowning. She can then rescue Marcus herself without Sofia making the situation worse.

Kant would object that Elena is using Sofia's ignorance to control her actions. Yet many people would consider the deception justified because it prevents immediate and serious harm. The lie is a temporary emergency measure to protect a vulnerable person, and Elena gains nothing from it. Still, the case does not prove that every protective lie is acceptable. A person might claim to lie "for someone's own good" when the real motive is embarrassment, convenience, or control. A lie should therefore be justified only when the danger is urgent, the harm is substantial, no truthful alternative is available, and the person lying accepts responsibility for the consequences. Kant's strict rule protects trust, but the lifeguard's dilemma shows that morality must also consider human vulnerability. In extreme cases, saving a life can outweigh an absolute ban on deception.

essay_student_17_sonnet.text:
Between 1849 and roughly 1860, Harriet Tubman made about thirteen return trips into the slaveholding South, and each one violated federal law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made it a crime to escape bondage or to help anyone else do so. It imposed fines up to $1,000 and jail time on abettors, denied accused fugitives a jury trial, and compelled ordinary citizens across the North to assist in captures on demand. Tubman had fled slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, in 1849. She answered the law by going back into the territory it was designed to police.

She traveled at night, often in winter when patrols were thinner and darkness lasted longer. She used the North Star and word-of-mouth contacts along what became known as the Underground Railroad to move people north. After 1850, the law's reach into free states meant Philadelphia and even New York were no longer safe endpoints, so she extended her routes to St. Catharines, Ontario, in Canada, where British law placed escapees beyond the reach of U.S. marshals. She is credited with personally leading around seventy enslaved people to freedom, including members of her own family. A bounty reportedly reaching $40,000 was rumored to hang over her capture.

The law assumed fear would seal the border in one direction. Tubman kept crossing it the other way, toward the greatest danger, to bring others out. She carried a pistol for self-protection and, according to later accounts, to press forward anyone who lost nerve and threatened to turn back and expose the group. During the Civil War she served as a scout and spy for the Union Army and helped lead the 1863 Combahee River raid in South Carolina, which freed over 700 enslaved people in a single night.

forum_answer_11_sonnet.text:
This happens because JavaScript stores numbers as IEEE 754 double-precision floats, and neither 0.1 nor 0.2 has an exact binary representation. Each is stored as the nearest approximable value. 0.1 is stored as roughly 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827, and 0.2 as roughly 0.200000000000000011102230246251565. Add those together and round to the nearest representable double, and you get 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. JavaScript isn't special here: Python, Java, C, and any other language using standard floating-point arithmetic give the same result (per IEEE 754). Try `0.1 + 0.2` in a Node.js console or your browser's devtools and you'll see it immediately.

For money, never use raw floats for arithmetic you plan to compare or sum precisely. A few solid options:

1. Work in integer cents or minor units. Store $19.99 as `1999`, do all math in integers, and only divide by 100 for display. This is the simplest fix and works fine until you need fractional cents or very large sums.

2. Use a decimal library. `decimal.js`, `big.js`, and `bignumber.js` model numbers as base-10 decimals instead of binary floats, so `0.1 + 0.2` really does equal `0.3`. For example, `new Decimal('0.1').plus('0.2').toString()` returns `"0.3"`.

3. Use native BigInt for whole-cent integer math if you don't need decimals mid-calculation. BigInt avoids float precision issues entirely for large integers.

4. Don't lean on `Number.prototype.toFixed()` either. It doesn't fix the underlying precision problem, it just rounds the display string, so use it for formatting only, not for actual calculations.

Rule of thumb: floats for measurements and graphics, integers or decimal libraries for money.

essay_student_15_glm.text:
Near the end of Mark Twain's *Adventures of Huckleberry Finn* (1884), Huck decides whether to send a letter to Miss Watson revealing the whereabouts of Jim, her escaped slave, or to "go to hell" and tear it up. When Huck scribbles the note to Jim's owner in Hannibal-based St. Petersburg, he feels momentarily "washed clean of sin." Then he remembers the thousand miles they have drifted down the Mississippi, the fog at Cairo, and Jim calling him "honey" and caring for him like a father. Holding the letter, Huck trembles, thinks of his brief prayer, and finally says, "All right, then, I'll go to hell." He tears the paper in two.

The moment matters because Huck's society has broken his conscience. He has been taught in Sunday school and by Widow Douglas that helping a slave escape is theft and damnation, so doing the "right thing" in his world means betraying his friend. Twain's irony is sharp: Huck judges himself a sinner precisely when he acts most morally. By choosing eternal punishment over Jim's re-enslavement, Huck rejects Miss Watson's property claim and, with it, an entire system of values. His moral growth lies in learning to trust the "sound heart" of his own experience over the "deformed conscience" of his culture, a phrase Twain himself used in an 1895 notebook to describe the novel's central conflict.

The decision is also a triumph of empathy over abstract rules. Huck cannot reason himself to abolitionism, since he has no political philosophy. What he has is memory: Jim mourning his daughter 'Lizabeth, whom he slapped before realizing she was deaf; Jim's joy at seeing Huck alive after the feud with the Grangerfords; the way the two of them argued about King Solomon and Frenchmen on the raft like family. Huck's ethics come from accumulated moments of shared humanity, with no doctrine behind them.

Critics rightly note that the novel's ending, where Tom Sawyer turns Jim's already-secured freedom into a game, undercuts Huck's growth. But it cannot erase it. When Huck chooses hell, Twain shows that a person builds conscience, choice by choice, from loyalty and love, instead of receiving it fixed from society.

Northwind Logistics' Q3 2026 strategy review shows solid progress on the Route 2027 electrification initiative, though charging infrastructure and vehicle lead times remain schedule risks.

As of September 15, the company has deployed 86 battery-electric delivery trucks across Seattle, Portland, and Sacramento. That is 43% of the 200-vehicle target for December 2027. The trucks completed 1.9 million route miles during the quarter, which reduced diesel consumption by approximately 410,000 gallons and avoided an estimated 3,700 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions. Fleet operations reported 94.2% vehicle availability, above the 92% program threshold, and average energy cost per mile was 28% below comparable diesel operations.

The largest gap is charging capacity. The Kent, Washington, depot operates 18 high-speed chargers, but permitting delays have pushed completion of 12 more from August to November 2026. Construction at the Tracy, California, facility remains on schedule for January 2027. Pacific Grid Solutions is contracted to install 24 chargers and a 4-megawatt battery-storage system there. Chief Operating Officer Elena Marquez has directed Facilities and Procurement to submit a contingency plan by October 10, covering temporary charging capacity and revised overnight dispatch procedures.

Capital spending through Q3 totaled $31.4 million against a full-year budget of $36 million. Finance expects the program to finish about $1.2 million over budget because of transformer costs and higher financing rates. Approved state and utility incentives of $2.6 million for the Washington and California sites will offset part of the overage.

For Q4, leadership approved the purchase of 38 more electric trucks, completion of the Kent expansion, and a driver training program starting October 24 in Portland. Human Resources will track technician certifications, safety incidents, and retention monthly. The executive steering committee will review Route 2027 again on January 18, 2027, and decide then whether to go ahead with the final 76-vehicle purchase.

reddit_post_06_luna.text:
I bought a Herman Miller Aeron (Remastered, Size B, graphite, with PostureFit SL) in March 2026 for $1,397 after tax. Six months later, I still can't decide whether it was a great investment or an extremely expensive placebo.

I work from home in Portland, Oregon, usually 8–10 hours a day as a project manager. Before the Aeron, I used a $250 Staples chair that made my lower back and shoulders ache by about 3 p.m. With the Aeron, the back pain is mostly gone. The mesh stays cool, the lumbar support really helps, and I no longer stand up feeling like I've been folded into a question mark.

It took me nearly three weeks to adjust, though. The seat felt too firm at first, and the hard frame edge bothered the backs of my thighs until I got the depth and tilt settings right. It also doesn't feel "luxurious" the way I expected for $1,400. My wife sat in it once and said it felt like "an ergonomic lawn chair."

My biggest complaint is that the arms squeak when I adjust them. The forward tilt is useful, but not as life-changing as reviews made it sound. I also still need to get up every hour, because no chair fixes sitting all day.

Overall, I'd rate it 8/10. It's comfortable, durable, and has noticeably improved my workdays, but I'm not sure it's four or five times better than a good $300–$500 chair.

If you own one: did you feel the same way after six months, or did the Aeron become more obviously worth it over time?

I'm 34F, and my neighbor "Karen" (42F) has a very friendly but completely unsupervised golden retriever named Murphy.

On Saturday, June 15, I spent most of the day planting a vegetable garden in my backyard in suburban Portland: six tomato plants, three zucchini plants, lettuce, peppers, and a row of herbs. Soil, seedlings, compost, and fencing cost me around $85, plus several hours of work.

On Monday morning I found Murphy in my yard. He had apparently squeezed through a gap in the fence while Karen was walking him. He dug up most of the garden, snapped the tomato plants, flattened the lettuce, and ate several peppers. Not everything was ruined, but I'd estimate about $50 worth of plants and supplies was destroyed.

I talked to Karen that evening and showed her photos. She apologized but said Murphy was "just being a dog," and offered to bring me some tomatoes from her grocery shopping. I told her I wasn't asking her to pay for my time, but $50 seemed fair to cover the actual damage. She got offended and said I was trying to "profit off an accident."

I then sent her a polite text explaining the costs and asking her to pay $50 by July 1. She now says I'm petty and that neighbors should be understanding. A couple of people on our street agree with her. They say dogs sometimes escape and I should let it go.

I don't want a feud, but I also don't think I should have to absorb the cost when her dog destroyed something that took me real money and hours to put together. AITA for asking her to reimburse me?

## Results

Tensile properties of Ti-6Al-4V specimens made by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) were evaluated at five laser powers (150, 175, 200, 225, and 250 W) on an EOS M290 system. Scan speed (1200 mm/s), hatch spacing (0.10 mm), and layer thickness (30 μm) were held constant. Ten dog-bone specimens (ASTM E8 subsize geometry) were printed per condition, stress-relieved at 650°C for 3 h under argon, and tested to failure on an Instron 5985 at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min.

Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) rose from 1021 ± 18 MPa at 150 W to a peak of 1147 ± 12 MPa at 200 W, then declined to 1089 ± 24 MPa at 225 W and 1043 ± 31 MPa at 250 W (mean ± SD, n = 10). A one-way ANOVA showed a significant effect of laser power on UTS (F(4,45) = 26.7, p < 0.001). Tukey HSD post hoc comparisons showed that the 200 W group differed significantly from every other group (p < 0.01) except 225 W (p = 0.08). Yield strength followed the same trend, peaking at 1068 ± 15 MPa at 200 W versus 948 ± 21 MPa at 150 W. Elongation at break was highest at 200 W (11.4 ± 0.9%) and dropped sharply at 250 W (6.2 ± 1.3%). Porosity rose over the same range, from 0.8% at 200 W to 2.9% at 250 W by micro-CT, and is attributed to keyhole-mode instability at higher energy density.

SEM fractography (Zeiss Sigma 300) of the 250 W specimens showed spherical keyhole pores, 30 to 80 μm in diameter, concentrated near the fracture initiation site, consistent with the reduced ductility. The 150 W specimens instead had irregular lack-of-fusion defects and lower UTS, even though their overall porosity (1.1%) was comparable. Within the tested range, and with the scan parameters fixed as in this study, 200 W gave the best balance of strength and ductility.

Considering a 15% pay cut to leave finance for a nonprofit: am I crazy?

I (34F) have worked in corporate finance at a mid-sized Chicago firm for 9 years and currently make $118k. Last week I got an offer from a nonprofit called Lakeside Community Health Partners for a Senior Financial Analyst role. It pays $100k, about a 15% cut.

My husband makes $85k as a teacher, our mortgage is $1,650/month, and we have about $40k left on student loans. No kids yet, but we plan to start trying next year. We have roughly $95k in savings and emergency funds.

Lakeside does healthcare access work on the South Side, and honestly, the mission is what's pulling me. At my current job I basically shuffle spreadsheets so execs can decide which vendors to squeeze. I'm good at it, but I come home feeling like I spent eight hours doing nothing that matters. When I interviewed at Lakeside, they said my forecasting work would directly support their three new community clinics opening in 2025. I got a little emotional, which has never happened in a finance interview.

What worries me:

1. The $18k difference is real money. It's what daycare would cost once we have a kid.
2. Nonprofit funding seems precarious. They told me they're grant-dependent, and one major federal grant comes up for renewal in March 2026.
3. Once you take a pay cut, is it hard to climb back if I hate it or need to return to corporate?

What's pulling me toward it: better hours (they said 40/week, versus my current 55+), a real mission, and a gut feeling I can't quite shake.

Has anyone here made a jump like this? Do you regret it, or was it the best decision you ever made? Is there anything I should ask Lakeside before signing, especially about that grant?

In March 2026, Customer Support received 63 customer complaint tickets. The largest issue was shipping delays at the Newark distribution hub, which accounted for about 26 tickets (41%). Customers most often reported that packages sat at the hub for several days without tracking updates, so they missed expected delivery dates and contacted Support again.

The delays were worst between March 10 and March 24, when multiple customers reported waits of three to seven business days. Affected orders shipped to New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Pennsylvania. Several customers also said their estimated delivery dates changed after checkout and the company did not notify them.

The other 37 complaints covered damaged packages, incorrect items, billing questions, and delivery-address issues. Each of these categories was smaller than the Newark delays. The Newark delays still posed the biggest risk to customer satisfaction because they hit one region and drew repeat contacts.

Customer Support now tags Newark-related tickets separately and escalates delayed shipments to the Logistics team each afternoon. Logistics is reviewing staffing, carrier pickup timing, and package-processing capacity at the hub. Support representatives are giving customers clearer explanations of the delay and confirming the next expected tracking update.

For April, the recommended priorities are a daily Newark delay dashboard, proactive customer notification when a shipment has been inactive for more than 48 hours, and a weekly review of hub performance with the primary carrier. Progress should be reassessed on April 15 and at month-end. The goal is to bring Newark-related complaints below 25% of total monthly tickets.

review_product_10_glm.text:
We stayed at the Ocean Coral & Turquesa beachfront property in Cancún for three nights, March 14–17, 2024. It was a mixed bag.

The location is the best part. Our sixth-floor room had a view of the turquoise water, and we fell asleep to the waves every night. The beach was clean, with plenty of palapas and loungers even when we came down after 10 a.m. The pool area was beautiful too, though the swim-up bar got crowded by noon.

The staff were lovely. Ricardo at the front desk checked us in quickly and suggested walking to Playa Delfines, about 15 minutes south, which turned out to be the highlight of our trip. Breakfast at the Las Olas buffet was solid: fresh fruit, made-to-order omelets, and the best chilaquiles I've had outside Mexico City.

The Wi-Fi was painfully slow, especially in the rooms. When I had to finish some work emails on our second day, uploading a handful of documents took almost 40 minutes. Speed tests showed 2–3 Mbps in the room. The lobby was better, maybe 10 Mbps, but who wants to sit in the lobby at 11 p.m.? The hotel advertises itself as business-friendly, so it should fix this.

There were smaller problems too. The air conditioning in our room rattled all night, and the elevator nearest our wing was out of service for two of our three days, which meant a long walk around the building with our suitcases. The à la carte Italian restaurant required a reservation, and we couldn't get one until our last night, which was frustrating.

Would we return? Probably, for the beach alone. Bring a book, though, and don't count on streaming anything. Three stars: great location and people, held back by tired infrastructure.

review_product_02_luna.text:
Christopher Nolan's *Oppenheimer* (2023) is an intense, ambitious film, and it works especially well in IMAX. The huge format makes the Trinity test sequence overwhelming: the silence before the explosion, the sudden flash of light, and the delayed roar produce a physical sense of dread more than spectacle. Ludwig Göransson's score and the pounding sound design add to this without making the film feel like a conventional action movie.

Cillian Murphy gives a strong performance as J. Robert Oppenheimer, who comes across as brilliant, vain, anxious, and increasingly haunted by the consequences of his work. The supporting cast is also very good, particularly Robert Downey Jr. as Lewis Strauss, Emily Blunt as Kitty Oppenheimer, and Matt Damon as General Leslie Groves. The shifting timelines and black-and-white sections feel complicated at first, but they gradually show how scientific achievement became entangled with politics, ego, and fear.

At three hours, *Oppenheimer* is long. Some courtroom and security-hearing scenes move slowly, and the dense dialogue demands concentration. Still, the runtime mostly feels justified, since the film covers the Manhattan Project, Oppenheimer's personal life, and the political fallout over several decades. In IMAX, the scale and detail make the length easier to accept, though it is worth taking a break beforehand. It is a demanding film rather than a relaxed historical drama, absorbing and exhausting, and it stayed with me after the credits.

review_product_12_sonnet.text:
I tried three recipes from Sarah Owens's *Sourdough* (Roost Books, 2015) over a rainy weekend in late August, using a starter I'd fed for exactly ten days beforehand.

The basic country loaf (p. 44) was the standout. It uses 72% hydration and a 4-hour bulk ferment at 78°F, and it came out of my Dutch oven with a real ear and open crumb on the first try.

The whole wheat sandwich loaf (p. 88) was fine but dense. I suspect my starter wasn't vigorous enough yet, since the book doesn't mention that this recipe depends on a starter that's been established for at least three weeks, not the ten days I gave mine.

The cinnamon-raisin swirl (p. 156) was a disaster. The dough tore every time I tried to shape it, and the instructions skip the lamination step entirely, saying only "roll and fill." Raisins burst through the crust in the oven.

The troubleshooting appendix (pp. 210-215) is where the book earns its keep. It correctly diagnosed my gummy interior as underbaking, not overproofing, and my second country loaf came out even better than the first.

Verdict: buy it for the country loaf and the troubleshooting section. Those two chapters are worth the $24.95 cover price. Skip the enriched doughs until your starter has a few more weeks on it, and don't attempt the swirl loaf without outside help. I had to watch a YouTube tutorial to fix my lamination technique before it worked.

**Fundraising Report: Spring Gala 2025**

To: Riverside Community Club Board of Directors
From: Maria Delgado, Fundraising Chair
Date: April 14, 2025
Re: Spring Gala results, final report

## Summary

The Spring Gala, held Saturday, April 5, at the Grandview Ballroom, netted $18,750 against our $15,000 target. That is 125% of our goal.

## Ticket sales

We sold 210 tickets at $75 each, for $15,750 in ticket revenue. That beat our projection of 190 tickets and last year's attendance of 188 guests (a 12% increase). Eighteen of the tickets were walk-in sales on the night, which I credit to our social media push in the final week.

## Revenue breakdown

- Ticket sales: $15,750
- Silent auction: $2,300
- Live auction (5 items): $1,900
- Raffle and wine pull: $850
- Total gross: $20,800

## Expenses

Expenses totaled $2,050: catering ($1,400), rentals ($350), and decorations ($300). Vista Catering discounted their services, and committee members donated all raffle and wine pull items. Net proceeds were $18,750.

## Highlights and acknowledgments

James Okafor emceed the live auction, which earned the most per item. The Lakeside Cabin weekend package alone brought in $700. The silent auction had 32 items donated by local businesses, a record for our club. Thanks also to the 14 volunteers who handled setup, check-in, and checkout.

## Recommendations

1. Raise the ticket price to $85 next year, since demand was strong and we sold out by April 1.
2. Expand the live auction to 8 items, based on this year's results.
3. Book the Grandview Ballroom by September, because 2026 spring dates are filling quickly.

Funds will be allocated as the board directs. The prior plan sent proceeds to the Youth Scholarship Program and clubhouse roof repairs.

Please contact me with any questions about the attached financial detail.
